- Ability to convert a Government scheme into realised benefit - management cites successful implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY) with meaningful monetary benefits secured
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer concentration and credit risk — Listed by the Company itself among its major risks. The Group states it is exposed to credit risk from operating activities, primarily trade receivables, plus loans receivable, investments and other financial instruments. Structurally acute for a staffing business that carries a large receivable book against a small number of large industrial clients: the segment note discloses that the single largest customer accounted for a double-digit share of total revenue in each of the last two years. Trade receivables are by far the largest financial asset on the Group's books.
- Cyclicality of client capital expenditure and project execution timelines — Company-flagged. Manpower demand is derived demand: a cyclical slowdown in capex by infrastructure, energy and industrial sectors, delays in EPC, oil & gas, manufacturing or renewable-energy projects, and slow client decision-making all translate directly into deployment gaps. Management explicitly links global geopolitical tension and commodity volatility to delayed capital expenditure and moderated hiring activity.
- Talent acquisition, retention and skill-gap risk — Company-flagged, and the sharpest structural risk for the model since the deployable engineer is the product. Demand for engineering, renewable energy, AI, semiconductor, digital and GCC talent is stated to outpace availability; the widening skill gap may intensify competition for qualified professionals, raise hiring costs and lengthen recruitment cycles.
- Margin compression from competitive intensity and rising employee costs — Company-flagged on both sides of the spread. The organised staffing industry faces intense competition from domestic, multinational and technology-enabled recruitment firms causing pricing pressure, while rising employee costs and inflationary pressures push the cost base up. This is a structural squeeze in a business whose largest single cost line is employee benefits.
- AI-led workforce disruption and technology obsolescence — Company-flagged. AI, automation and digital technologies may reduce demand for routine and repetitive roles even as they raise demand for high-skilled professionals. Management states staffing companies must continuously adapt talent strategies, technology capabilities and recruitment processes; failure to do so is an existential risk to a deputation-volume model.
- Regulatory and labour-law change — Company-flagged. Changes in labour regulations, employment law, taxation, social security requirements and compliance frameworks directly alter workforce management economics and raise compliance obligations for staffing companies and their clients. A staffing intermediary bears this risk on behalf of its clients.
- Foreign exchange exposure and geopolitical risk in overseas markets — Company-flagged in the MD&A as forex fluctuations affecting international operations plus geopolitical developments in overseas markets. NOTE A CONTRADICTION IN THE AR: the Ind AS financial-risk note asserts 'The Group does not have significant foreign currency exposure and hence is not exposed to any significant foreign currency risks', yet the same note discloses unhedged foreign-currency trade receivables outstanding at March 31, 2026 in USD, GBP, QAR and SAR, and separately states there were NO derivative instruments outstanding at either March 31, 2026 or March 31, 2025 - i.e. the exposure is entirely unhedged. With international expansion an explicit strategic priority, this risk is directionally increasing while the note describes it as insignificant.
- Cybersecurity and information technology risk — Company-flagged, tied to digital operations and technology-enabled recruitment platforms. Management states it proactively updates digital verification systems to address emerging cybersecurity and compliance risks as industrial plants and GCC clients modernise. A staffing business holds large volumes of candidate and employee personal data, making this both an operational and a regulatory exposure.
- Liquidity and working-capital risk — Disclosed in the Ind AS financial-risk note: the Group monitors shortage-of-funds risk on a regular basis and seeks to balance continuity of funding with flexibility through cash credit facilities. Relevant because a staffing business pays deployed manpower monthly while collecting from industrial clients on longer terms; management separately cites tighter working capital management and better collections as a FY26 improvement lever, confirming this is an actively managed pressure point. The 'Working Capital Position' discussion is truncated out of the routed text.
- Single-segment and geographic concentration — A structural concentration risk that the AR does not label as a risk. The Company states it has only ONE reportable operating segment - Manpower Supply and Consultancy Services - so there is no diversifying second business line, and the standalone entity's international turnover is stated to be a very small fraction of total turnover, meaning the standalone book is overwhelmingly India-exposed even as the group targets 20% international. The disclosed medium-term mix target of 60/20/20 is itself an acknowledgement that today's concentration is higher than desired.
- Interest rate risk - stated as not significant — The Ind AS note states the Group does not have significant debt obligation with floating interest rates and hence is not exposed to any significant interest rate risk. Recorded as a stated management assertion, which is a real disclosure and not silence; the Group does carry borrowings, so the assertion rests on their being fixed-rate rather than on absence of debt.

business.body: Established in 1987 and headquartered in Mumbai, Aarvi Encon supplies specialised engineering and technical manpower and project-support services across the entire project lifecycle - from engineering and procurement through construction, commissioning, operations and maintenance. The Company serves industrial and infrastructure clients through technical staffing, manpower outsourcing, engineering services, O&M deployment, permanent recruitment and IT staffing, operating a pan-India network alongside a growing international presence in the Middle East and Southeast Asia. The segment note states the Company has only one reportable operating segment, Manpower Supply and Consultancy Services.

outlook.body:
- Build a balanced and resilient business portfolio over the medium term by strengthening the core staffing business, expanding higher-value service offerings, and increasing international presence.
- Achieve a business mix of approximately 60% India Staffing Services, 20% India Operation & Maintenance (O&M) Services and 20% International Business, which management states will enhance profitability, strengthen recurring revenue streams and improve resilience across business cycles.
- Increase the contribution of higher-margin O&M services within the overall business portfolio to improve earnings quality.
- Expand international operations across the Middle East and Southeast Asia, pursued with stated prudence, discipline and a long-term perspective; maintain a balanced mix of domestic and international operations so the business can perform across economic cycles.
- Develop the new Chennai engineering office into a dedicated engineering centre to strengthen India engineering support and project execution capability.
- Expand in renewable energy by deploying specialised technical manpower for O&M across solar module and solar cell manufacturing projects.
- Invest in technology and digital capabilities, strengthen engineering capabilities and develop the workforce to adapt to digitalisation, automation, AI and sustainability reshaping engineering services.
- Move from supplying manpower toward delivering dependable integrated solutions with speed, quality and accountability, as customers increasingly demand.
- Maintain disciplined financial management and profitable growth rather than growth for its own sake, protecting financial strength and capital structure.
- Strengthen governance as a base for long-term plans - internal financial controls, compliance processes, financial reporting systems and the enterprise risk management framework were all reinforced during the year.
- Continue CSR focus on healthcare, education, environmental sustainability, women empowerment and community development.
- The Board voluntarily adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy on May 29, 2023, which sets out the parameters and circumstances the Board takes into account in determining distribution of dividend to shareholders. Acting on the Company's performance, that policy and shareholders' interest, the Board at its meeting on May 22, 2026 recommended a final dividend for the year ended March 31, 2026, payable within 30 days of shareholder approval to members on the register as at the end of Friday, August 7, 2026; declaration of that final dividend is tabled as Ordinary Business item 3 at the 38th AGM to be held on Friday, August 14, 2026 through VC/OAVM. (The per-share amount and the stated outflow are recorded under profile.commitments rather than repeated here, since this field is specified as policy intent rather than figures.) The stated underlying philosophy, from the Executive Director & CFO, is profitable rather than indiscriminate growth - 'We have never believed in growth for its own sake' - protecting financial strength, disciplined financial management, tighter working capital management and better collections to improve financial flexibility, and keeping the capital structure healthy while retaining room to invest in future opportunities including technology, digital capabilities and people. Reinvestment intent is directed at the Chennai engineering centre, international footprint expansion and higher-margin O&M capability. Shares continue to be issued in small tranches under the Aarvi Encon Limited Employee Stock Option Plan, 2022. The Company has also formulated a Policy for determining Material Subsidiaries and a Nomination and Remuneration Policy, both published on its website. No buyback, no debt-reduction target and no credit rating is disclosed in the routed governance text.
- CSR focus areas stated by both the Managing Director and the Executive Director & CFO: healthcare, education, environmental sustainability, women empowerment and community development.
- Named CSR beneficiary organisations supported during the year: Saifee Hospital, SankalpTaru Foundation and Shree Kasturba Stri Vikasgruh.
- Governance/ESG framing: the Code of Conduct is described as the principal document capturing the core Corporate Governance and ESG principles, and the Company states it aims to comply with all requirements of law in letter and spirit by adopting 'best-in-class ESG practices'.
- Vigil Mechanism Policy in place under Regulation 22 of the Listing Regulations and Section 177(9) of the Act, covering violations of legal or regulatory requirements, misrepresentation of financial statements, unethical behaviour and actual or suspected fraud, with safeguards against victimisation and direct access to the Chairman of the Audit Committee. STATED NIL: no such complaints were received during the year.
- Board diversity: one Woman Independent Director on a six-member Board as at March 31, 2026; Independent Directors held a separate meeting on March 23, 2026 to evaluate the Chairman, non-independent directors and the Board as a whole.
- Social/employment contribution: management cites successful implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY), a Government employment-generation scheme, under which the Company secured monetary benefits.
- Stated forward intent to maintain strong corporate governance, compliance standards and sustainable business practices, and continued investment in human capital, upskilling and people development.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Aarvi Encon is an asset-light services business and the routed text discloses no plants, no installed capacity and no rupee capex quantum. Expansion is expressed entirely as footprint, delivery capability and headcount. In India, the Company established a new engineering office in Chennai during FY 2025-26, which it states is expected to enhance engineering support and project execution capabilities, and which it aims to develop into a dedicated engineering centre with a team of approximately 500 professionals over the next three to four years. Internationally, the Company opened a new office in Malaysia during the year to support its growing international business, secured manpower and engineering services contracts in the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia, and continued efforts to stabilise operations in Qatar, alongside existing presence in Oman, Saudi Arabia and the wider Middle East and Southeast Asia. Aarvi Encon FZE, the wholly owned subsidiary incorporated in the SAIF Zone, Sharjah, UAE, continues to be a Material Subsidiary under Regulation 16 of the Listing Regulations as its net worth exceeds ten percent of consolidated net worth. Vertical expansion during the year came from deploying specialised technical manpower for O&M activities across solar module and solar cell manufacturing projects, alongside a stated intent to keep increasing the share of higher-margin O&M within the portfolio. The stated forward footprint priorities are expanding domestic and international presence, strengthening the Operations & Maintenance and Engineering Services businesses, increasing participation in renewable energy and manufacturing sectors, leveraging technology to improve recruitment efficiency and operational productivity, and diversifying the customer base and service offerings. A corporate-history milestone infographic in the Corporate Overview also references opening a subsidiary in UAE, partnering with Bon Accord Employment Services in UAE, opening branch offices in Oman and Indonesia, acquiring M N R Technical Staffing Company in Dubai, an O&M services start with HMPL, a DHDS and SRU commissioning contract from HPCL Refinery, a CRISIL 'SME-1' rating, listing on the NSE Emerge platform and a subsequent main-board listing; the year labels and event text in that infographic were de-interleaved by the text extraction, so individual year-to-event pairings are NOT reliable and no dates are asserted here.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's continued focus on infrastructure creation, manufacturing, renewable energy, industrial growth and employment generation is stated to create a strong demand environment for specialised engineering talent.
- Growing international presence gives access to attractive markets and new sources of growth; a balanced domestic-international mix is stated to make the business better placed to perform across different economic cycles.
- International business was a key growth driver during the year, with contracts secured in the UAE and Indonesia, a new office in Malaysia, and efforts continuing to stabilise operations in Qatar, alongside presence in Oman and Saudi Arabia.
- Growth drivers cited for the year: an expanding customer base, deeper engagement with existing clients, improved execution capabilities, and rising demand for specialised engineering, technical manpower and integrated workforce solutions across diverse industries.
- Margin lever: shifting mix toward higher-margin O&M services, supporting improved earnings quality; also disciplined execution, better operating efficiency and careful financial management.
- Working capital lever: management states operating cash flows improved on tighter working capital management, better collections and prudent use of resources, improving financial flexibility.
- Government scheme benefit: management cites successful implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana (PM-VBRY), under which the Company secured meaningful monetary benefits.
- Industry structure - global: the staffing and recruitment industry is expanding on demand for skilled professionals, workforce flexibility and technology-enabled hiring; companies with domain expertise, technology-enabled recruitment, global delivery models and scalable solutions are expected to play an increasingly strategic role.
- Industry structure - India: growth supported by favourable demographics, workforce formalisation, rapid digitalisation, GCC expansion, PLI-linked manufacturing investment, infrastructure development and wider adoption of flexible staffing and RPO.
- Demand breadth: staffing demand stated as robust across engineering, infrastructure, manufacturing, IT, BFSI, healthcare, logistics, retail, renewable energy and Global Capability Centres.
- Macro backdrop cited by management: IMF global growth of approximately 3.1% in CY2026; MoSPI India real GDP growth of 7.7% in FY2025-26; RBI projecting around 6.6% growth in FY2026-27; CPI moderating to about 3.4% in March 2026 and the repo rate at 5.25% in June 2026. Geopolitical tension, commodity price volatility, trade policy and financial market volatility are named as key monitorable risks.
- Structural technology shift: AI, automation, predictive analytics and skills-based hiring are reshaping recruitment; localisation of supply chains is raising skilled-talent demand in India, Southeast Asia and the Middle East.
- No order book, order inflow or pipeline value is disclosed anywhere in the routed strategy/outlook text - the Company reports no quantified order book.
- Qualitative pipeline evidence only: 'During the year, we secured important manpower and engineering services contracts in the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia, further strengthening our presence in these markets.' No contract value, duration or count is stated.
